questions.prompt: Are there more or fewer than 8,000 hours in a year?
questions.fact: 365 days × 24 hours = 8,760 hours.

source.name: Worked out by Hunchy's own code

questions.prompt: What is half of a quarter?
questions.fact: Half of 1/4 is 1/8.

source.name: Worked out by Hunchy's own code

questions.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?
questions.fact: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Battle of Hastings take place?
questions.fact: William of Normandy beat King Harold II at Hastings in 1066 and became William the Conqueror.

questions.prompt: Which king of England was forced to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.fact: King John sealed the Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215. It limited the king's power for the first time.

questions.prompt: How many wives did King Henry VIII have?
questions.fact: Henry VIII married six times. A rhyme helps remember their fates: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

questions.prompt: In which year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.fact: Columbus landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, on a voyage paid for by Spain.

questions.prompt: Which famous fire destroyed much of the City of London in 1666?
questions.fact: The Great Fire of London started in a bakery on Pudding Lane in September 1666 and burned for about four days.

questions.prompt: Did the Great Fire of London start in a bakery?
questions.fact: It began at Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane in the early hours of 2 September 1666.

questions.prompt: Who tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605?
questions.fact: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the gunpowder on 5 November 1605. That's why Bonfire Night is on 5 November.

questions.prompt: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated?
questions.fact: Elizabeth I's navy, helped by storms, beat Spain's great fleet of ships in 1588.

questions.prompt: Which city was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?
questions.fact: Ash from Vesuvius buried Pompeii so quickly that streets, homes and even loaves of bread were preserved.

questions.prompt: On which day in 44 BC was Julius Caesar killed?
questions.fact: Caesar was stabbed by Roman senators on the Ides of March, 15 March, 44 BC.

questions.prompt: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall built across northern Britain?
questions.fact: Building of Hadrian's Wall began in AD 122. Parts of it still stand today.

questions.prompt: Whose tomb did Howard Carter find in Egypt's Valley of the Kings in 1922?
questions.fact: Tutankhamun's tomb was found almost untouched, packed with treasures including his famous gold mask.

questions.prompt: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Was Stonehenge's first stage built earlier or later?
questions.fact: The first stage of Stonehenge, a circular ditch and bank, was built around 3000 BC, a few centuries before the Great Pyramid.

questions.prompt: Which country did Germany invade on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War in Europe?
questions.fact: Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on 3 September 1939.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Second World War end?
questions.fact: The war in Europe ended in May 1945, and in Asia in August, with Japan's formal surrender on 2 September 1945.

questions.prompt: In which year did the First World War begin?
questions.fact: The war began in the summer of 1914 and ended with an armistice on 11 November 1918.

questions.prompt: Did the First World War end with an armistice at 11 o'clock on the 11th day of the 11th month?
questions.fact: The guns fell silent at 11am on 11 November 1918. That's why Remembrance Day is held on 11 November.

questions.prompt: Whose assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 helped spark the First World War?
questions.fact: Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

source.name: Wikipedia: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

questions.prompt: What was the code name for the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day, 6 June 1944?
questions.fact: Overlord was the whole invasion. The landings on the beaches themselves were called Operation Neptune.

questions.prompt: During the Second World War, which battle was fought in the skies over southern England in 1940?
questions.fact: The RAF fought the German air force from July to October 1940, stopping a planned invasion.

questions.prompt: In 1940, more than 330,000 soldiers were rescued from the beaches of which French town?
questions.fact: Hundreds of small boats, many owned by ordinary people, helped the navy carry soldiers home from Dunkirk.

questions.prompt: Which American naval base was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941?
questions.fact: The attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii brought the United States into the Second World War.

questions.prompt: In which city did Anne Frank hide with her family during the Second World War?
questions.fact: Anne Frank wrote her famous diary while hiding in a secret annexe in Amsterdam from 1942 to 1944.

questions.prompt: Who was Britain's prime minister for most of the Second World War?
questions.fact: Churchill became prime minister in May 1940 and led Britain until July 1945.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.fact: The border opened on the night of 9 November 1989, and Germany was reunited the next year.

source.name: Wikipedia: Fall of the Berlin Wall

questions.prompt: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989. Was it first built before or after 1960?
questions.fact: Building began on 13 August 1961, so the wall stood for 28 years.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Titanic sink?
questions.fact: The Titanic hit an iceberg on its first voyage and sank in the early hours of 15 April 1912.

questions.prompt: Was the Titanic on its very first voyage when it sank?
questions.fact: It had set off from Southampton on its maiden voyage to New York.

questions.prompt: In which year did people first walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

questions.prompt: In which year did the French Revolution begin with the storming of the Bastille?
questions.fact: Crowds stormed the Bastille prison in Paris on 14 July 1789. France still celebrates 14 July as its national day.

questions.prompt: Which famous battle in 1815 ended Napoleon's rule for good?
questions.fact: Wellington's British-led army and the Prussians beat Napoleon at Waterloo, in what is now Belgium.

questions.prompt: At which sea battle in 1805 was Admiral Nelson killed?
questions.fact: Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar but was shot during it. Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square remembers him.

questions.prompt: In which year did the United States declare its independence from Britain?
questions.fact: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776, which is why Americans celebrate the Fourth of July.

source.name: Wikipedia: United States Declaration of Independence

questions.prompt: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.fact: Factories, steam engines and new machines spread across Britain from the second half of the 1700s.

questions.prompt: Who were the first people to fly a powered aeroplane, in 1903?
questions.fact: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903. The first flight lasted 12 seconds.

questions.prompt: Queen Victoria reigned for 63 years. Did Queen Elizabeth II reign for longer or shorter?
questions.fact: Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years, from 1952 to 2022: longer than any other British monarch.

questions.prompt: Which group of Scandinavian raiders attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793?
questions.fact: The raid on Lindisfarne, off the coast of Northumberland, is often taken as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

questions.prompt: Which terrible disease killed a huge share of Europe's people in the late 1340s?
questions.fact: The Black Death, a plague, killed somewhere between a third and a half of Europe's population.

questions.prompt: Who was released from prison in 1990 and became South Africa's president in 1994?
questions.fact: Mandela spent 27 years in prison. He became South Africa's first Black president.

questions.prompt: Which American civil rights campaigner made the 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
questions.fact: He gave the speech to about 250,000 people at the March on Washington on 28 August 1963.

questions.prompt: Did Rosa Parks refuse to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955?
questions.fact: Her arrest led to the Montgomery bus boycott, a turning point in the American civil rights movement.

questions.prompt: In which year did a nuclear reactor explode at Chernobyl?
questions.fact: Reactor 4 at Chernobyl, in what is now Ukraine, exploded on 26 April 1986.

questions.prompt: Which crisis in 1962 brought the USA and the Soviet Union close to nuclear war?
questions.fact: For 13 days in October 1962 the world held its breath over Soviet missiles in Cuba.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Channel Tunnel between England and France open?
questions.fact: The tunnel opened in May 1994. Its rail tunnels are about 50 km long, with about 38 km under the sea.

questions.prompt: In which year did euro notes and coins first go into people's pockets?
questions.fact: The euro started for banks in 1999. Notes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002.

questions.prompt: In 1893, which became the first self-governing country to let all women vote in national elections?
questions.fact: New Zealand women won the right to vote in national elections in 1893, decades before most of the world.

source.name: Wikipedia: Women's suffrage in New Zealand

questions.prompt: Who led the Allied armies in Europe on D-Day and later became US president?
questions.fact: Eisenhower was Supreme Commander of the Allied forces in Europe, and US president from 1953 to 1961.

questions.prompt: The ancient Olympic Games were held in Greece.
questions.fact: They were held at Olympia, in honour of the god Zeus. The first recorded Games are traditionally dated to 776 BC.

questions.prompt: Which ancient wonder was a giant statue standing at a harbour on a Greek island?
questions.fact: The bronze Colossus stood on Rhodes for only about 54 years before an earthquake toppled it in 226 BC.

questions.prompt: In 1773, colonists angry about British taxes threw tea into the harbour of which American city?
questions.fact: The Boston Tea Party saw 342 chests of tea thrown into the harbour. It was a step towards the American Revolution.

questions.prompt: Who was Britain's first woman prime minister?
questions.fact: Margaret Thatcher was prime minister from 1979 to 1990, longer than anyone else in the 20th century.

questions.prompt: Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in 1979. Did Tony Blair become prime minister before or after 2000?
questions.fact: Tony Blair became prime minister in May 1997 and served until 2007.

questions.prompt: Which British prime minister called the 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union?
questions.fact: David Cameron called the referendum and resigned the morning after the vote to leave.

questions.prompt: Who is usually counted as Britain's first prime minister?
questions.fact: Sir Robert Walpole led the government from 1721 to 1742, and is generally regarded as the first prime minister.

questions.prompt: What is the address of the British prime minister's official home in London?
questions.fact: Robert Walpole moved into Number 10 in 1735. It has been the prime minister's home and office ever since.

questions.prompt: Who was the first president of the United States?
questions.fact: George Washington became president in 1789. The capital city, Washington D.C., is named after him.

questions.prompt: Which US president issued the Emancipation Proclamation and gave the Gettysburg Address?
questions.fact: Lincoln was the 16th president. He led the country through the American Civil War and pushed through the end of slavery.

questions.prompt: Who was the first Black president of the United States?
questions.fact: Barack Obama was the 44th president, from 2009 to 2017.

questions.prompt: Which US president was assassinated in Dallas in 1963?
questions.fact: John F. Kennedy was shot in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963.

questions.prompt: Who was the US president when astronauts first landed on the Moon in 1969?
questions.fact: Nixon spoke to Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin by phone while they were on the Moon.

questions.prompt: Which US president had been a Hollywood film actor?
questions.fact: Ronald Reagan acted in dozens of films before going into politics. He was president from 1981 to 1989.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to be Chancellor of Germany?
questions.fact: Angela Merkel led Germany for 16 years, from 2005 to 2021.

questions.prompt: Which Indian leader led a peaceful campaign for independence from Britain?
questions.fact: Gandhi led protests without violence, like the 1930 Salt March. India became independent in 1947.

questions.prompt: Who crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804?
questions.fact: Napoleon took the crown from the Pope's hands and placed it on his own head at Notre-Dame in Paris.

questions.prompt: Who was the last active ruler of ancient Egypt's Ptolemaic kingdom?
questions.fact: Cleopatra VII ruled Egypt until her death in 30 BC, after which Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.

questions.prompt: Which queen ruled England when Shakespeare's first plays were performed?
questions.fact: Elizabeth I reigned from 1558 to 1603, a golden age for English theatre.

questions.prompt: In which year was King Charles III crowned at Westminster Abbey?
questions.fact: Charles became king in September 2022. His coronation was on 6 May 2023.

source.name: Wikipedia: Coronation of Charles III and Camilla

questions.prompt: Who was Britain's longest-reigning monarch?
questions.fact: Queen Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years, from 1952 until her death in 2022.

questions.prompt: Queen Victoria became queen when she was 18 years old.
questions.fact: Victoria came to the throne in 1837, a month after her 18th birthday.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to become president of a country in a national election, in Iceland in 1980?
questions.fact: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir served as Iceland's president for 16 years.

questions.prompt: Which scientist came up with the famous equation E = mc²?
questions.fact: Einstein published it in 1905. It shows that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: Marie Curie won in 1903 for physics, and again in 1911 for chemistry.

questions.prompt: Did Marie Curie win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
questions.fact: She won the physics prize in 1903 and the chemistry prize in 1911. She is still the only person to win in two different sciences.

questions.prompt: Which scientist is famous for a story about an apple and gravity?
questions.fact: Newton said that watching an apple fall helped him think about gravity. The apple tree still grows at his home, Woolsthorpe Manor.

questions.prompt: Which naturalist sailed on HMS Beagle and wrote On the Origin of Species?
questions.fact: Darwin's voyage lasted almost five years. His book about evolution came out in 1859.

questions.prompt: Which nurse became known as 'The Lady with the Lamp'?
questions.fact: Florence Nightingale cared for soldiers in the Crimean War and went on to found modern nursing.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, followed by Buzz Aldrin about 20 minutes later.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean?
questions.fact: Amelia Earhart flew from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 1932.

questions.prompt: Which mathematician is often called the first computer programmer?
questions.fact: In the 1840s Ada Lovelace wrote what is seen as the first program, for Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine.

questions.prompt: Which mathematician helped break the Enigma code in the Second World War?
questions.fact: Alan Turing worked at Bletchley Park. He is on the Bank of England's £50 note.

questions.prompt: In which town was William Shakespeare born?
questions.fact: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564. You can still visit the house he was born in.

questions.prompt: Who wrote A Christmas Carol, the story of Ebenezer Scrooge?
questions.fact: Dickens wrote it in just six weeks. It was published on 19 December 1843 and sold out by Christmas Eve.

questions.prompt: In which year was the first Harry Potter book published?
questions.fact: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was first published in the UK in June 1997.

source.name: Wikipedia: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

questions.prompt: Who wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory?
questions.fact: Roald Dahl's book first came out in 1964. He also wrote Matilda, The BFG and The Witches.

source.name: Wikipedia: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory

questions.prompt: Who wrote The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe?
questions.fact: It came out in 1950, the first of the seven Chronicles of Narnia books to be published.

source.name: Wikipedia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

questions.prompt: Who wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings?
questions.fact: The Hobbit came out in 1937. Tolkien was a professor of English at Oxford.

questions.prompt: Which explorer led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
questions.fact: Amundsen's Norwegian team got there on 14 December 1911, about five weeks before Scott's British team.

questions.prompt: Who first reached the top of Mount Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953?
questions.fact: The New Zealander Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay reached the summit on 29 May 1953.

questions.prompt: Which British scientist invented the World Wide Web?
questions.fact: Tim Berners-Lee came up with the idea in 1989 while working at CERN in Switzerland.

questions.prompt: Which famous naturalist presented the TV series Blue Planet and Planet Earth?
questions.fact: David Attenborough has made nature films for the BBC for more than 70 years.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.fact: The Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface, more than all the land put together.

questions.prompt: What is the highest mountain above sea level?
questions.fact: Everest's official height, agreed by China and Nepal in 2020, is 8,848.86 metres.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.fact: The Sahara covers about 9 million km² of North Africa. Antarctica, a cold desert, is even bigger.

questions.prompt: Is Antarctica counted as a desert?
questions.fact: A desert is a place with very little rain or snow. Antarctica gets so little that it is the largest desert on Earth.

questions.prompt: How many continents are there, in the way most countries teach it?
questions.fact: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (or Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.

questions.prompt: Which is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
questions.fact: The Severn runs about 354 km from the Welsh mountains to the Bristol Channel. The Thames is second.

questions.prompt: What is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
questions.fact: Ben Nevis, in the Scottish Highlands, is 1,345 metres high.

questions.prompt: Which river flows through Paris?
questions.fact: The Seine flows through the middle of Paris, under 37 bridges.

questions.prompt: Which line of latitude runs around the middle of the Earth?
questions.fact: The Equator is about 40,075 km long and divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest island in the world (not counting Australia)?
questions.fact: Greenland covers about 2.2 million km². Australia is counted as a continent rather than an island.

questions.prompt: The Eiffel Tower is about 330 metres tall. Is the Shard in London taller or shorter?
questions.fact: The Shard is 310 metres tall, the tallest building in the UK.

questions.prompt: What is the tallest building in the world?
questions.fact: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is 828 metres tall. It opened in 2010.

questions.prompt: The Burj Khalifa is 828 metres tall. Is the Empire State Building, to its tip, more or less than half that height?
questions.fact: The Empire State Building is 443 metres to the tip of its antenna, a little over half the height of the Burj Khalifa.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Colosseum?
questions.fact: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 and could hold about 50,000 spectators.

questions.prompt: In which country is Machu Picchu?
questions.fact: Machu Picchu is an Inca city high in the Andes mountains, built in the 1400s.

questions.prompt: In which Indian city is the Taj Mahal?
questions.fact: The emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.prompt: Which city is home to the Sydney Opera House?
questions.fact: It opened in 1973. Its roof looks like sails on the harbour.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
questions.fact: The statue was a gift from France and was put up in New York Harbor in 1886.

questions.prompt: Was the Statue of Liberty a gift from France?
questions.fact: The people of France gave it to the United States. It was designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi.

questions.prompt: What colour was the Statue of Liberty when it was first put up?
questions.fact: It was the colour of a shiny new penny. The copper slowly turned green as it reacted with the air, until it was fully green by about 1920.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the great bell inside London's famous clock tower?
questions.fact: Big Ben is really the bell. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Leaning Tower?
questions.fact: The tower began to lean while it was still being built, in the 1170s, because the ground underneath was too soft.

questions.prompt: Which city has canals instead of streets and gondolas instead of taxis?
questions.fact: Venice is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon, linked by about 400 bridges.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Sagrada Família, a church still being built more than a century after it was started?
questions.fact: Work began in 1882. The architect Antoni Gaudí spent the last 43 years of his life on it.

questions.prompt: Which is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid is also the oldest of the seven, built about 4,500 years ago.

source.name: Wikipedia: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

questions.prompt: You can see the Great Wall of China from the Moon with your own eyes.
questions.fact: That's a myth. The wall is long but very narrow, and astronauts say it can't be seen from the Moon.

questions.prompt: In which city is the famous Christ the Redeemer statue?
questions.fact: The statue stands on top of Corcovado mountain, looking out over Rio. It was finished in 1931.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the famous red bridge in San Francisco?
questions.fact: The Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937. Its colour is called International Orange.

questions.prompt: Tower Bridge in London opened in 1894. Did the Golden Gate Bridge open earlier or later?
questions.fact: The Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937, 43 years after Tower Bridge.

questions.prompt: In which city would you find the Brandenburg Gate?
questions.fact: The gate stood right next to the Berlin Wall and became a symbol of Germany reunited.

questions.prompt: Which famous museum has a glass pyramid at its entrance?
questions.fact: The glass pyramid, designed by I. M. Pei, opened in 1989.

questions.prompt: Which ancient stone circle stands on Salisbury Plain in England?
questions.fact: Stonehenge was built in stages over about 1,500 years, starting around 3000 BC.

questions.prompt: Which city is known as the Big Apple?
questions.fact: The nickname was made popular by a 1970s tourism campaign, though it was used decades earlier.

questions.prompt: Which city is known as the City of Light?
questions.fact: Paris earned the name as a centre of ideas and learning, and for being one of the first cities with gas street lights.

questions.prompt: Which London landmark is a giant observation wheel on the South Bank?
questions.fact: The London Eye opened in 2000. A full turn takes about 30 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which city hosted the Olympic Games in 2012?
questions.fact: London became the first city to host the modern Summer Olympics three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

questions.prompt: Which city is the capital of Scotland?
questions.fact: Edinburgh Castle sits on the rock of an old volcano in the middle of the city.

questions.prompt: Which city is the capital of Wales?
questions.fact: Cardiff has been the capital of Wales since 1955.

questions.prompt: Which city is the capital of Northern Ireland?
questions.fact: The Titanic was built in Belfast, at the Harland and Wolff shipyard.

questions.prompt: Which city has the most people in the world, counting its whole urban area?
questions.fact: A United Nations report in late 2025, using a new way of measuring cities, put Jakarta top with nearly 42 million people, ahead of Dhaka and Tokyo.

source.name: UN DESA: Latest urbanization data reveal world's most populous cities

questions.prompt: In which city is the Kremlin?
questions.fact: The Kremlin is a walled fortress in the centre of Moscow. Next to it is Red Square.

questions.prompt: Which city is split between two continents, Europe and Asia?
questions.fact: The Bosphorus strait runs through Istanbul, with Europe on one side and Asia on the other.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Acropolis?
questions.fact: The Parthenon, a temple to the goddess Athena, stands on the Acropolis. It was finished in 432 BC.

questions.prompt: Which Dutch city is famous for its canals and the Anne Frank House?
questions.fact: Amsterdam's ring of 17th-century canals is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.prompt: Which Scottish lake is famous for stories about a monster?
questions.fact: Loch Ness is so deep, about 230 metres, that it holds more fresh water than all the lakes in England and Wales put together.

questions.prompt: Which famous medieval clock in Prague's Old Town Square shows the positions of the Sun and Moon?
questions.fact: Prague's Astronomical Clock was first installed in 1410. It is the oldest one still working.

questions.prompt: Which city is home to the Little Mermaid statue?
questions.fact: The statue, unveiled in 1913, is based on Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale.

questions.prompt: Which American city is home to Hollywood?
questions.fact: The Hollywood sign first went up in 1923 and originally said HOLLYWOODLAND.

questions.prompt: Big Ben's clock tower is 96 metres tall. Is the Leaning Tower of Pisa taller or shorter?
questions.fact: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is about 56 metres tall on its high side.

questions.prompt: In which year was the Eiffel Tower finished?
questions.fact: It was built for the 1889 World's Fair, marking 100 years since the French Revolution. It was meant to stand for only 20 years.

questions.prompt: In which country is Petra, the ancient city carved into pink rock?
questions.fact: Petra was carved by the Nabataeans more than 2,000 years ago. It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

questions.prompt: In which country are the Maya pyramids of Chichén Itzá?
questions.fact: The great pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps if you count the top platform: one for each day of the year.

questions.prompt: Which canal links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?
questions.fact: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. It saves ships sailing all the way round Africa.

questions.prompt: Which canal lets ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
questions.fact: The Panama Canal opened in 1914. Locks lift ships about 26 metres up to a lake and back down again.

questions.prompt: In which city is Times Square, famous for its giant screens and New Year's Eve ball drop?
questions.fact: Times Square is named after The New York Times, which moved there in 1904.

questions.prompt: What is H₂O better known as?
questions.fact: Each water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

questions.prompt: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
questions.fact: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, and give off oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe?
questions.fact: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

questions.prompt: At what temperature does pure water boil at sea level?
questions.fact: Water boils at 100 °C, or 212 °F. High up a mountain the air pressure is lower, so it boils at a lower temperature.

questions.prompt: What is the hardest natural material?
questions.fact: Diamond is pure carbon, the same element as the graphite in a pencil, just arranged differently.

questions.prompt: How many bones does an adult human body have?
questions.fact: Babies are born with nearer 300, but some join together as they grow.

questions.prompt: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.fact: An adult's skin weighs about 4 kg and covers about 2 m².

questions.prompt: Which part of the body pumps blood around it?
questions.fact: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times a day.

questions.prompt: Where in the body is the smallest bone?
questions.fact: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is about 3 mm long.

questions.prompt: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air. Does light travel faster or slower?
questions.fact: Light travels at nearly 300,000 km per second, almost a million times faster than sound. That's why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

questions.prompt: How long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 150 million km away, so its light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us.

questions.prompt: Which scientist's name is used for the unit of force?
questions.fact: One newton is about the force of a small apple pressing down in your hand.

questions.prompt: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
questions.fact: Bees turn sugary nectar into honey. They also carry pollen, which helps plants make seeds.

questions.prompt: What colour do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
questions.fact: Blue and yellow paint make green. Mixing coloured light works differently: red and green light make yellow.

questions.prompt: How many colours are traditionally named in a rainbow?
questions.fact: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Isaac Newton chose seven names.

questions.prompt: A magnet's north pole pulls towards another magnet's north pole.
questions.fact: Like poles push apart. A north pole pulls towards a south pole.

questions.prompt: What does DNA carry?
options: The instructions for building living things
questions.fact: DNA is a long molecule, shaped like a twisted ladder, found in nearly every cell.

questions.prompt: Which famous shape is the DNA molecule?
questions.fact: James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix in 1953, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin.

questions.prompt: Who discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928?
questions.fact: Fleming noticed that mould on a dish had killed the bacteria around it.

questions.prompt: Who made the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796?
questions.fact: Jenner used cowpox to protect people against smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.prompt: Is a tomato a fruit, scientifically speaking?
questions.fact: A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds, so tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers are all fruits.

questions.prompt: What is the freezing point of water in Fahrenheit?
questions.fact: Water freezes at 0 °C, which is 32 °F.

questions.prompt: Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C. Is the boiling point of water higher or lower than three times that?
questions.fact: Three times 37 is 111 °C, and water boils at 100 °C.

questions.fact: No Viking helmet with horns has ever been found. The idea mostly comes from costumes for operas in the 1800s.

questions.prompt: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years later, and about 2,000 years before the Moon landing.

questions.prompt: Was Napoleon unusually short for a man of his time?
questions.fact: Napoleon was about 1.69 metres tall, about average for a Frenchman then. British cartoons made fun of him as tiny.

questions.prompt: Which age came straight after the Stone Age?
questions.fact: Bronze is made by mixing copper and tin. The Iron Age came after the Bronze Age.

questions.prompt: Which ancient wonder was a giant lighthouse in Egypt?
questions.fact: It stood for well over 1,000 years before earthquakes brought it down.

questions.prompt: Which Mongol leader founded the largest land empire in history?
questions.fact: Kublai Khan was his grandson, who went on to rule China.

questions.prompt: Which English queen ruled for only about nine days in 1553?
questions.fact: Lady Jane Grey was pushed aside by Mary I, Henry VIII's daughter.

questions.prompt: Which king of Scotland also became King James I of England in 1603?
questions.fact: When Elizabeth I died without children, James joined the two crowns.

questions.prompt: Who became the world's first woman prime minister, in Sri Lanka in 1960?
questions.fact: Sri Lanka was called Ceylon at the time.

questions.prompt: Who was India's first prime minister?
questions.fact: Nehru led India from independence in 1947 until 1964.

questions.prompt: Which US president was the first to live in the White House?
questions.fact: George Washington chose the site, but the house wasn't ready until 1800, when John Adams moved in.

questions.prompt: How many years is a US president elected for?
questions.fact: A US president can only be elected twice.

source.name: Wikipedia: President of the United States

questions.prompt: Who was the youngest person ever elected president of the United States?
questions.fact: Kennedy was 43 when elected in 1960. Theodore Roosevelt was younger when he took over, but he wasn't elected at first.

questions.prompt: Which French president gave his name to Paris's biggest airport?
questions.fact: Pompidou gave his name to the Centre Pompidou, a modern art museum in Paris.

questions.prompt: On which island did Nelson Mandela spend 18 of his 27 years in prison?
questions.fact: Robben Island, off Cape Town, is now a museum.

questions.prompt: Jacinda Ardern was prime minister of which country?
questions.fact: She led New Zealand from 2017 to 2023.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to lead Pakistan?
questions.fact: Benazir Bhutto became prime minister in 1988, aged 35.

questions.prompt: Who was Britain's prime minister when the Second World War began in 1939?
questions.fact: Churchill took over in May 1940.

questions.prompt: Was Queen Victoria on the throne when Winston Churchill was born?
questions.fact: Churchill was born in 1874. Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901.

questions.prompt: Which explorer gave his name to the Americas?
questions.fact: A German map of 1507 was the first to use the name America.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
questions.fact: The play is set in Verona, Italy.

questions.prompt: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.fact: Conan Doyle was a doctor, and based Holmes partly on one of his teachers in Edinburgh.

questions.prompt: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
questions.fact: It came out in 1813. Jane Austen is on the Bank of England £10 note.

questions.prompt: Who wrote The Gruffalo?
questions.fact: Axel Scheffler drew the pictures. The book came out in 1999.

questions.prompt: Which scientist wrote A Brief History of Time?
questions.fact: The book, from 1988, has sold more than 25 million copies.

source.name: Wikipedia: A Brief History of Time

questions.prompt: Who first climbed Everest without bottled oxygen, with Peter Habeler in 1978?
questions.fact: Messner went on to climb all 14 of the world's mountains over 8,000 metres.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to swim the English Channel, in 1875?
questions.fact: Captain Webb took nearly 22 hours. Gertrude Ederle was the first woman, in 1926.

questions.prompt: Who is the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: Malala won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014, aged 17, for standing up for girls' education.

questions.prompt: Who was the last tsar of Russia?
questions.fact: Nicholas II gave up the throne in 1917.

questions.prompt: Which explorer was the first European to see the east coast of Australia, in 1770?
questions.fact: Cook sailed on HMS Endeavour. Dutch sailors had reached Australia's west coast earlier.

questions.prompt: Which scientist set out three laws of motion in 1687?
questions.fact: His first law says that things keep still, or keep moving in a straight line, unless a force acts on them.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to fly over the English Channel in an aeroplane, in 1909?
questions.fact: The flight from Calais to Dover took about 37 minutes.

questions.prompt: What is gold's chemical symbol?
questions.fact: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold. Ag is silver.

questions.prompt: How many teeth does an adult usually have, including wisdom teeth?
questions.fact: Children have 20 baby teeth.

questions.prompt: Which blood cells help fight infection?
questions.fact: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Platelets help blood clot when you cut yourself.

questions.prompt: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.fact: Below 7 is acid, like lemon juice. Above 7 is alkaline, like soap.

questions.prompt: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level. At the top of Everest, does it boil at a higher or lower temperature?
questions.fact: The air pressure is much lower up there, so water boils at about 70 °C. Tea comes out weak.

questions.prompt: Which element is there more of in the universe than any other?
questions.fact: About three-quarters of the normal matter in the universe is hydrogen.

source.name: Wikipedia: Abundance of the chemical elements

questions.prompt: What does a barometer measure?
questions.fact: Falling air pressure often means rain is on the way.

questions.prompt: Which part of a plant makes most of its food?
questions.fact: Leaves use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make sugar. This is called photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin does your skin make in sunlight?
questions.fact: Vitamin D helps keep bones and teeth strong.

questions.prompt: Roughly how fast does light travel?
questions.fact: Light could go round the Earth about seven times in one second.

questions.prompt: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
questions.fact: Tall buildings get hit again and again. The Empire State Building is struck about 20 times a year.

questions.prompt: Who arranged the first periodic table of the elements, in 1869?
questions.fact: Mendeleev left gaps for elements nobody had found yet, and predicted what they would be like.

questions.prompt: What is the centre of an atom called?
questions.fact: Electrons whizz around the nucleus, which holds protons and neutrons.

questions.prompt: Are old church and castle windows thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows?
questions.fact: Old glass was uneven when it was made, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Glass doesn't flow at room temperature.

questions.prompt: Which gas do we breathe out more of than we breathe in?
questions.fact: Our bodies use oxygen and make carbon dioxide as waste.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first dog to orbit the Earth, in 1957?
questions.fact: Laika flew on the Soviet Sputnik 2. Belka and Strelka orbited and came home safely in 1960.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the most known moons?
questions.fact: Astronomers keep finding more small moons around Saturn. It has well over 200.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the giant volcano on Mars, the biggest in the Solar System?
questions.fact: Olympus Mons is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

questions.prompt: Which Moon mission had an explosion on the way in 1970, but brought its crew home safely?
questions.fact: The crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat. The film Apollo 13 came out in 1995.

questions.prompt: Which company makes the Falcon 9 rocket?
questions.fact: Falcon 9's first stage lands back on Earth so it can be used again.

questions.prompt: A day on Earth lasts 24 hours. Is a day on Jupiter longer or shorter?
questions.fact: Jupiter spins once in about 10 hours, even though it's by far the biggest planet.

questions.prompt: Which colour of star is the hottest?
questions.fact: Red stars are the coolest. Our Sun is yellow-white, in the middle.

questions.prompt: There is no gravity on the International Space Station.
questions.fact: Gravity up there is about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they're always falling around the Earth.

questions.prompt: What is a shooting star really?
options: A bit of space rock burning up in the air
questions.fact: Most shooting stars are made by pieces of dust or rock smaller than a grain of sand.

questions.prompt: Which space telescope, launched in 1990, is named after an American astronomer?
questions.fact: Edwin Hubble showed that there are other galaxies beyond our own.

questions.prompt: Which NASA rover landed on Mars in 2021, carrying a little helicopter?
questions.fact: The helicopter, Ingenuity, made the first powered flight on another planet.

questions.prompt: Which famous comet comes back past the Earth about every 76 years?
questions.fact: It was last seen in 1986 and is due back in 2061.

questions.prompt: What is a group of owls called?
questions.fact: A pride is lions, a murder is crows and a school is fish.

source.name: Wikipedia: List of English terms of venery, by animal

questions.prompt: How many legs does a crab have, counting its claws?
questions.fact: Crabs are decapods, which means 'ten feet'.

questions.prompt: A cheetah can reach about 100 km/h. Can a greyhound run faster or slower?
questions.fact: A greyhound tops out at about 70 km/h. It's still the fastest dog.

questions.prompt: What is a baby swan called?
questions.fact: A gosling is a baby goose.

questions.prompt: Which is the biggest member of the cat family?
questions.fact: Siberian tigers are the biggest of all and can weigh more than 300 kg.

questions.prompt: Do snails have teeth?
questions.fact: A snail has thousands of tiny teeth on a ribbon-like tongue called a radula.

questions.prompt: Why are flamingos pink?
options: Because of the food they eat
questions.fact: Flamingo chicks are grey. They turn pink from colours in the shrimp and algae they eat.

questions.prompt: How many arms does a starfish usually have?
questions.fact: Some kinds have many more, and a starfish can grow a lost arm back.

questions.prompt: Which tree do acorns grow on?
questions.fact: Conkers come from the horse chestnut tree.

questions.prompt: Is a strawberry a berry, in the way botanists use the word?
questions.fact: Botanically, a strawberry isn't a berry, but bananas and grapes are.

questions.prompt: What is a male bee called?
questions.fact: Drones don't sting and don't collect food. The worker bees are female.

questions.prompt: Which animal has fingerprints so like ours that they're hard to tell apart, even under a microscope?
questions.fact: Koalas and humans developed fingerprints separately, probably for gripping.

questions.prompt: Goldfish can only remember things for three seconds.
questions.fact: Studies show goldfish can remember things for months, and can even be trained.

questions.prompt: Which is the only mammal that can truly fly?
questions.fact: Flying squirrels and sugar gliders only glide.

questions.prompt: Which bird lays the biggest eggs?
questions.fact: An ostrich egg weighs about as much as 24 hens' eggs.

questions.prompt: Which band's song 'Mr. Brightside' has stayed in the UK charts for years?
questions.fact: The Killers come from Las Vegas. 'Mr. Brightside' first came out in 2003.

questions.prompt: Which instrument usually has 47 strings and seven pedals?
questions.fact: The pedals change the pitch of the strings so the harp can play in any key.

questions.prompt: Which Beatles album cover shows the band walking over a zebra crossing?
questions.fact: The crossing is outside the Abbey Road Studios in London and is a listed site.

questions.prompt: Which singer is known as the Queen of Pop?
questions.fact: Madonna is the best-selling female solo artist of all time.

questions.prompt: Who sang 'Purple Rain'?
questions.fact: Purple Rain was also a film, in 1984.

questions.prompt: Bono is the lead singer of which Irish band?
questions.fact: U2 formed in Dublin in 1976, when its members were still at school.

questions.prompt: Which rapper's real name is Marshall Mathers?
questions.fact: Eminem comes from M and M, his initials.

questions.prompt: Who sang 'Uptown Funk' with Mark Ronson?
questions.fact: It was one of the biggest hits of 2015.

questions.fact: Despacito means 'slowly'. Its video was the first on YouTube to pass 5 billion views.

questions.prompt: Which family of instruments does the trumpet belong to?
questions.fact: The saxophone is made of brass, but it counts as woodwind because it uses a reed.

questions.prompt: The Beatles' first UK single came out in 1962. Did the Rolling Stones release their first single earlier or later?
questions.fact: The Rolling Stones' first single, 'Come On', came out in 1963.

questions.prompt: Which singer was known as the Queen of Soul?
questions.fact: Her hit 'Respect' came out in 1967.

questions.prompt: What does an orchestra's conductor usually hold?
questions.fact: The baton helps the players see the beat from far away.

questions.prompt: Which singer from Barbados had a huge hit with 'Umbrella'?
questions.fact: 'Umbrella' was number one in the UK for ten weeks in 2007.

questions.prompt: Which group was Beyoncé in before she went solo?
questions.fact: Destiny's Child had hits with 'Survivor' and 'Say My Name'.

questions.prompt: How many lines are there in a musical stave?
questions.fact: Notes sit on the lines or in the spaces between them.

questions.prompt: How many musicians play in a quartet?
questions.fact: A string quartet has two violins, a viola and a cello.

questions.prompt: Which composer wrote the piano piece 'Für Elise'?
questions.fact: Nobody is sure who Elise was. The piece wasn't published until 40 years after Beethoven died.

questions.prompt: Which instrument did Jimi Hendrix famously play?
questions.fact: Hendrix was left-handed and played a right-handed guitar upside down.

questions.prompt: Which singer's fans call themselves Swifties?
questions.fact: Taylor Swift started out as a country singer in Nashville.

questions.prompt: Who plays Captain Jack Sparrow in Pirates of the Caribbean?
questions.fact: The films were inspired by a ride at Disneyland.

questions.prompt: In which film does a great white shark terrorise the town of Amity Island?
questions.fact: Jaws, from 1975, is often called the first summer blockbuster.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the school of witchcraft and wizardry in Harry Potter?
questions.fact: Beauxbatons and Durmstrang are rival schools in Harry Potter. Nevermore is Wednesday Addams's school.

questions.prompt: In The Wizard of Oz, which character wants a brain?
questions.fact: The Tin Man wants a heart and the Lion wants courage.

questions.fact: Bonnie Wright played Ginny Weasley.

questions.fact: The Hobbiton set in Matamata is now a place you can visit.

questions.prompt: Which hobbit does Elijah Wood play in The Lord of the Rings?
questions.fact: Bilbo, Frodo's uncle, found the ring in The Hobbit.

questions.fact: Superman is Clark Kent, Spider-Man is Peter Parker and Iron Man is Tony Stark.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Thor's hammer in the Marvel films?
questions.fact: Stormbreaker is the axe Thor gets later, in Avengers: Infinity War.

questions.prompt: On which TV quiz show do players hear the line 'Is that your final answer'?
options: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?
questions.fact: The show began on ITV in 1998 and has been copied in more than 100 countries.

source.name: Wikipedia: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? (British game show)

questions.prompt: Which dinosaur chases the jeep in Jurassic Park?
questions.fact: The famous ripple in a glass of water warns that the T. rex is coming.

questions.prompt: Who plays Mr Brown in the Paddington films?
questions.fact: Hugh Grant played the villain, Phoenix Buchanan, in Paddington 2.

questions.prompt: Who plays Willy Wonka in the 2023 film Wonka?
questions.fact: Gene Wilder played Wonka in 1971 and Johnny Depp in 2005.

questions.prompt: Mamma Mia! is set on an island in which country?
questions.fact: Much of it was filmed on the Greek island of Skopelos. The songs are all by ABBA.

questions.fact: Martin Freeman played his friend Dr Watson.

questions.prompt: The first Toy Story came out in 1995. Did the first Shrek come out more or less than five years later?
questions.fact: Shrek came out in 2001, six years after Toy Story.

questions.prompt: Which TV series is set in a land called Westeros?
questions.fact: It was filmed in many places, including Northern Ireland, Croatia and Iceland.

questions.fact: Monk's Café is the diner in Seinfeld.

questions.fact: Ian Fleming, who wrote the books, worked in naval intelligence during the Second World War.

questions.prompt: In The Lion King, which song do Timon and Pumbaa teach Simba?
options: I Just Can't Wait to Be King
questions.fact: Hakuna matata is Swahili for 'no worries'.

questions.prompt: How many letters are there in the English alphabet?
questions.fact: They come from the Latin alphabet. J, U and W were added much later than the rest.

questions.prompt: Which letter is used most often in written English?
questions.fact: E turns up in about one in every eight letters. T and A come next.

questions.prompt: Which alphabet is used to write Russian?
questions.fact: Cyrillic is also used for Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and many other languages.

questions.prompt: Which of these languages is written from right to left?
questions.fact: Hebrew and Persian are written from right to left too, though numbers usually run left to right.

questions.prompt: The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two letters of which alphabet?
questions.fact: Alpha and beta are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.

questions.prompt: What is the last letter of the Greek alphabet?
questions.fact: That's why 'alpha and omega' means the beginning and the end.

questions.prompt: How many letters does the Hawaiian alphabet have?
questions.fact: Five vowels, seven consonants and the ʻokina, a mark that stands for a short pause in the voice.

questions.prompt: Is the letter Q always followed by a U in English words?
questions.fact: Words such as Qatar, Iraqi and qwerty break the rule, and Scrabble players love 'qi'.

source.name: Wikipedia: List of English words containing Q not followed by U

questions.prompt: What is the QWERTY keyboard named after?
options: The first six letters on its top row of letters
questions.fact: The layout dates from typewriters in the 1870s.

questions.prompt: In the NATO radio alphabet, which word stands for the letter Z?
questions.fact: The alphabet runs Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, and so on, so letters can't be misheard over a crackly radio.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'kindergarten' come from?
questions.fact: It means 'children's garden'. Friedrich Fröbel opened the first one in Germany in 1837.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'shampoo' come from?
questions.fact: It comes from a word meaning 'to press or knead'. Sake Dean Mahomed opened shampooing baths in Brighton in 1814.

questions.prompt: The word 'robot' was first used in a play from 1920. Which language does it come from?
questions.fact: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. used it, from 'robota', meaning forced labour. His brother Josef suggested the word.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'tsunami' come from?
questions.fact: It means 'harbour wave'.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'safari' come from?
questions.fact: In Swahili, safari simply means 'journey'.

questions.prompt: The word 'avocado' comes, through Spanish, from which language?
options: Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs
questions.fact: The Aztec word was āhuacatl. Tomato and chilli come from Nahuatl too.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'algebra' come from?
questions.fact: It comes from 'al-jabr' in the title of a maths book written in Baghdad in the 800s.

questions.prompt: The word 'bungalow' comes from a word meaning 'from Bengal' in which language?
questions.fact: British people in India used it for low, single-storey houses with a veranda.

questions.prompt: Do we know for certain where the word 'quiz' comes from?
questions.fact: A famous story says a Dublin theatre manager chalked 'quiz' on walls to win a bet, but there's no evidence for it. Its origin is still a mystery.

questions.prompt: Which of these words is first recorded in Shakespeare's plays?
questions.fact: Shakespeare is also credited with 'swagger', 'fashionable' and 'uncomfortable'.

source.name: Mental Floss: 21 words created by Shakespeare

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'ski' come from?
questions.fact: It comes from an Old Norse word for a split piece of wood.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'yoghurt' come from?
questions.fact: It comes from a Turkish word meaning to knead or thicken.

questions.prompt: Which language does the word 'cookie' come from?
questions.fact: It comes from 'koekje', meaning 'little cake'.

questions.prompt: Does the word 'emoji' come from the English word 'emotion'?
questions.fact: It's Japanese: 'e' means picture and 'moji' means character. The likeness to 'emotion' is a happy accident.

questions.prompt: What does 'karaoke' mean in Japanese?
questions.fact: The music plays without a singer, leaving the space for you.

questions.prompt: The radio distress call 'Mayday' comes from which language?
questions.fact: It comes from 'm'aider', as in 'come and help me'. It was chosen in 1923 by a radio officer at Croydon airport.

questions.prompt: Which word was Oxford Dictionaries' Word of the Year in 2013?
questions.fact: Vape was chosen in 2014.

questions.prompt: Did a word that doesn't mean anything once get printed in a major dictionary by mistake?
questions.fact: 'Dord' appeared in Webster's dictionary in 1934, after a note saying 'D or d' was misread. It stayed for years before anyone noticed.

questions.prompt: 'Piano' is short for 'pianoforte'. What does that mean in Italian?
questions.fact: Earlier keyboards couldn't change volume. The pianoforte could play softly or loudly depending on how hard you pressed.

questions.prompt: What is the main language of Brazil?
questions.fact: Brazil has more Portuguese speakers than Portugal, by about 20 times.

questions.prompt: Wales has two official languages. Does Switzerland have more or fewer national languages?
questions.fact: Switzerland has four: German, French, Italian and Romansh.

questions.prompt: In which country is Afrikaans mainly spoken?
questions.fact: Afrikaans grew out of Dutch, so Dutch and Afrikaans speakers can often understand each other.

questions.prompt: How many official languages does the United Nations use?
questions.fact: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.

source.name: Wikipedia: Official languages of the United Nations

questions.prompt: What is the national language of Pakistan?
questions.fact: English is an official language there too.

questions.prompt: In which country is Catalan the only official language?
questions.fact: In Spain, Catalan is official in Catalonia alongside Spanish.

questions.prompt: Basque is spoken in parts of Spain and France. Which language is it related to?
questions.fact: Basque is a 'language isolate': no link to any other living language has been proved.

questions.prompt: What does 'déjà vu' mean in French?
questions.fact: It's the strange feeling that you've lived a moment before.

questions.prompt: In Italian, what does 'ciao' mean?
questions.fact: It comes from an old Venetian phrase meaning 'I am your slave', said as a friendly 'at your service'.

questions.prompt: The German word 'Handschuh' means 'hand shoe'. What is it?
questions.fact: German is full of words built like this. A 'Kühlschrank', a 'cool cupboard', is a fridge.

questions.prompt: What do Americans call the boot of a car?
questions.fact: Americans call the bonnet the hood.

questions.prompt: What do Americans call a full stop?
questions.fact: Americans also say 'period' at the end of a sentence to mean 'and that's final'.

questions.prompt: What do you call a word that reads the same backwards, like 'level'?
questions.fact: 'Racecar' and 'kayak' are palindromes too.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not an anagram of 'listen'?
questions.fact: An anagram uses exactly the same letters. 'Listed' swaps the N for a D.

questions.prompt: Which pair of words are homophones?
questions.fact: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.

questions.prompt: Is 'scuba' short for something?
questions.fact: It stands for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

questions.prompt: What does the A in LASER stand for?
questions.fact: LASER is short for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

questions.prompt: What does 'i.e.' mean?
questions.fact: It's short for the Latin 'id est'. 'For example' is e.g.

questions.prompt: Which is usually called the longest word in major English dictionaries?
questions.fact: It's a lung disease caused by breathing in very fine dust. It was invented in 1935 to be the longest word.

questions.prompt: 'Antidisestablishmentarianism' has 28 letters. Does 'pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis' have more or fewer?
questions.fact: It has 45 letters.

questions.prompt: What is a group of flamingos called?
questions.fact: A pride is lions, a parliament is owls and a pod is whales or dolphins.

source.name: Wikipedia: List of English terms of venery, by animal

questions.prompt: What is a group of whales called?
questions.fact: A shoal is fish.

source.name: Wikipedia: List of English terms of venery, by animal

questions.prompt: In English Scrabble, which two letters are worth 10 points?
questions.fact: J and X are worth 8.

questions.prompt: How many tiles are there in a standard English Scrabble set?
questions.fact: Two of them are blanks, which can stand for any letter.

questions.prompt: What is the word for a word that sounds like what it describes, such as 'buzz'?
questions.fact: 'Sizzle', 'pop' and 'splash' are onomatopoeia too.

questions.prompt: 'She sells seashells by the seashore' is an example of what?
questions.fact: Alliteration repeats the same sound at the start of words close together.

questions.prompt: What do you call a word that means the opposite of another, like 'hot' and 'cold'?
questions.fact: A synonym means the same, like 'big' and 'large'.

questions.prompt: Which word turns up more often than any other in written English?
questions.fact: 'The' makes up roughly one in every 20 words people write. 'Be' and 'to' come next in most counts.

source.name: Wikipedia: Most common words in English

questions.prompt: A haiku has 3 lines. Does a limerick have more or fewer?
questions.fact: A limerick has 5 lines, and the first, second and fifth rhyme.

questions.prompt: How many lines does a sonnet have?
questions.fact: Shakespeare wrote 154 of them.

questions.prompt: What does 'www' stand for at the start of a web address?
questions.fact: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989.
